### Problem: Non-overlapping intervals {#sec-pf-p3-intervals}

::: {.p-statement}
Given $n$ intervals $[s_i, e_i)$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$), return the minimum number to remove so that the rest do not overlap. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint do not overlap.

Source: [LC 435 · Non-overlapping Intervals](https://leetcode.com/problems/non-overlapping-intervals/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Removing the fewest is keeping the most: this is activity selection. Keep the interval that **ends first**, because it leaves the most room for the rest.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
Sort by end; keep an interval when its start is $\ge$ the end of the last kept one. Answer $= n - $ kept.

**Exchange proof.** Let $g$ be the interval with the smallest end, and $O$ an optimal set of kept intervals whose first interval (by end) is $o_1 \ne g$. Replace $o_1$ by $g$: since $\text{end}(g) \le \text{end}(o_1) \le \text{start}(o_2)$, the set stays non-overlapping and has the same size. So some optimal solution starts with $g$. Remove $g$ and every interval overlapping it; the remaining problem is the same problem on fewer intervals, and induction finishes the proof.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: pf-intervals
def erase_overlap(intervals):
    kept, last_end = 0, -math.inf
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[1]):
        if s >= last_end:
            kept, last_end = kept + 1, e
    return len(intervals) - kept

def erase_overlap_brute(intervals):
    n = len(intervals)
    for keep in range(n, -1, -1):
        for subset in combinations(sorted(intervals), keep):
            if all(subset[i][1] <= subset[i + 1][0] for i in range(keep - 1)):
                return n - keep

def random_intervals(n):
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        s = random.randint(0, 15)
        out.append((s, s + random.randint(1, 6)))
    return out

for _ in range(1000):
    iv = random_intervals(random.randint(0, 9))
    assert erase_overlap(iv) == erase_overlap_brute(iv)

assert erase_overlap([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (1, 3)]) == 1
assert erase_overlap([(1, 2), (1, 2), (1, 2)]) == 2
assert erase_overlap([(1, 2), (2, 3)]) == 0

# Wrong keys are caught immediately by the same brute force:
def greedy_by(key, intervals):
    kept, chosen = 0, []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=key):
        if all(e <= cs or s >= ce for cs, ce in chosen):
            chosen.append((s, e)); kept += 1
    return len(intervals) - kept
assert greedy_by(lambda iv: iv[0], [(0, 10), (1, 2), (3, 4)]) == 2        # by start: keeps (0,10), wrong
assert greedy_by(lambda iv: iv[1] - iv[0], [(0, 4), (3, 6), (5, 9)]) == 2  # by length: keeps (3,6), wrong
assert erase_overlap([(0, 4), (3, 6), (5, 9)]) == 1
```

#### C++

```cpp
int eraseOverlapIntervals(vector<vector<int>>& iv) {
    sort(iv.begin(), iv.end(), [](auto& a, auto& b) { return a[1] < b[1]; });
    int kept = 0;
    long long lastEnd = LLONG_MIN;
    for (auto& v : iv)
        if (v[0] >= lastEnd) { ++kept; lastEnd = v[1]; }
    return (int)iv.size() - kept;
}
```
:::

::: {#fig-pf-intervals}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
sample = [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (1, 3)]
kept, last = [], -math.inf
for s, e in sorted(sample, key=lambda iv: iv[1]):
    kept.append(s >= last)
    if s >= last:
        last = e
assert kept.count(False) == erase_overlap(sample) == 1
def draw(ax, p):
    items = [(s, e, f"[{s},{e})", "green" if k else "red", not k)
             for (s, e), k in zip(sorted(sample, key=lambda iv: iv[1]), kept)]
    V.intervals(ax, p, items, scale=1.6, row_h=0.6)
V.show(draw)
```

The sample [(1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (1,3)] sorted by end. Greedy keeps the green intervals and removes the dashed one: 1 removal.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(n\log n)$ for sorting, $O(n)$ for the scan. **Space** $O(1)$ beyond the sort.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Touching intervals (`[1,2)` and `[2,3)`) are compatible: use `>=`, not `>`.
- Duplicate intervals: all but one must go.
- Sorting by start, or by length, is wrong; the counterexamples are in the code.
:::
